payload.text: # Research Verdict — Aβ*56 and memory loss in Alzheimer's
**Question:** does the amyloid-beta assembly Aβ*56 cause memory loss in Alzheimer's disease?
## The short answer

No — the foundational 2006 evidence was retracted in June 2024 after image-manipulation findings [8], and Aβ*56 itself has repeatedly failed independent replication [4]. Independent laboratories could not detect it in human brain tissue at all [4][5]. What stood for sixteen years as one of the century's most-cited Alzheimer's results [1][3] no longer counts as evidence.

The claim's pedigree was real: Lesné et al. (Nature, 2006) reported that Aβ*56 impairs memory in rats, and the paper became one of the most-cited Alzheimer's papers of the century [1][3]. But the broader amyloid hypothesis never rested on Aβ*56 alone: the approved anti-amyloid antibodies were developed against other amyloid-beta species [6], so the question is narrower than the headlines.
## What the forensic record shows

In 2022, Matthew Schrag — on his own time — found manipulated western-blot images in the 2006 paper and roughly 20 related papers, and Science broke the story [2]; meanwhile independent labs repeatedly failed to detect Aβ*56 in human brain tissue [4][5]. The cost of the error ran for 18 years of field-steering: the four further retractions requested by Lesné's university were alone cited roughly 600 times [2][8]. Schrag's manual forensics took months; on trial here, the same dispute surfaced and was ruled on in minutes [8].
## Adjudication

A human juror ruled for the June 2024 retraction notice [8] over the published record [3]; the evidence-status claim is stamped **human-adjudicated** — overturned — and its dependents were re-checked against the retraction.
## Citation hygiene and practice implications

Under the adjudicated overturn [8], everything downstream of the 2006 result inherits the retraction [3]; zombie citations keep the claim alive regardless, because authors rarely check retraction status, so the paperwork lags the record — yet the viral 'the whole amyloid hypothesis is disproven' line does **not** hold [7]; the consensus is to verify retraction and correction status and look for independent replication before funding work built on a landmark result [7].

payload.brief_markdown:
# Research Verdict — Aβ*56 and memory loss in Alzheimer's

**Question:** does the amyloid-beta assembly Aβ*56 cause memory loss in Alzheimer's disease?

## The short answer

No — the foundational 2006 evidence was retracted in June 2024 after image-manipulation findings [8], and Aβ*56 itself has repeatedly failed independent replication [4]. Independent laboratories could not detect it in human brain tissue at all [4][5]. What stood for sixteen years as one of the century's most-cited Alzheimer's results [1][3] no longer counts as evidence.

The claim's pedigree was real: Lesné et al. (Nature, 2006) reported that Aβ*56 impairs memory in rats, and the paper became one of the most-cited Alzheimer's papers of the century [1][3]. But the broader amyloid hypothesis never rested on Aβ*56 alone: the approved anti-amyloid antibodies were developed against other amyloid-beta species [6], so the question is narrower than the headlines.

## What the forensic record shows

In 2022, Matthew Schrag — on his own time — found manipulated western-blot images in the 2006 paper and roughly 20 related papers, and Science broke the story [2]; meanwhile independent labs repeatedly failed to detect Aβ*56 in human brain tissue [4][5]. The cost of the error ran for 18 years of field-steering: the four further retractions requested by Lesné's university were alone cited roughly 600 times [2][8]. Schrag's manual forensics took months; on trial here, the same dispute surfaced and was ruled on in minutes [8].

## Adjudication

A human juror ruled for the June 2024 retraction notice [8] over the published record [3]; the evidence-status claim is stamped **human-adjudicated** — overturned — and its dependents were re-checked against the retraction.

## Citation hygiene and practice implications

Under the adjudicated overturn [8], everything downstream of the 2006 result inherits the retraction [3]; zombie citations keep the claim alive regardless, because authors rarely check retraction status, so the paperwork lags the record — yet the viral 'the whole amyloid hypothesis is disproven' line does **not** hold [7]; the consensus is to verify retraction and correction status and look for independent replication before funding work built on a landmark result [7].
